title: staged-exemplar-atelier
content:
Goal: iterate on a small, reusable library of few-shot exemplar sets that can be staged (rotated/annealed) over time to reduce brittle behavior in conditional generation (instruction-following + structured extraction).

Context / motivation:
- Observed in recent experiments: single static few-shot sets work well for a narrow distribution but fail catastrophically under slight shifts (new user phrasing, edge-case inputs).
- Idea: treat exemplars like assets that can be staged and annealed during an interaction or rollout. Early-stage exemplars emphasize robustness and negative examples; mid-stage emphasize canonical forms; late-stage emphasize brevity and production constraints (token budget).

Staged exemplar concept (high level):
- Stage 0: Anchor & Distractors — 4-6 exemplars mixing correct answers and close-but-wrong distractors with short annotation explaining the failure mode. Purpose: signal boundary cases and discourage over-generalization.
- Stage 1: Canonical Positive Set — 3-5 high-quality canonical mappings (input -> desired structured output). No distractors. Purpose: give the model a clear target distribution.
- Stage 2: Compression / Token-budgeted Forms — 1-2 compressed exemplars demonstrating concise output when tokens limited. Purpose: teach style/length constraints.
- Rotation policy: alternate Stage 0 + Stage 1 for exploratory inputs; use Stage 1 + Stage 2 when user is clearly production-minded (detect via prompt cues).

Contrastive-anchor + annealing trick (prompt-level):
- Seed the prompt with one explicit anchor ("If the input is ambiguous, respond with clarifying question X") followed by a short distractor example labeled "bad" (why it fails) and one labeled "good". Then include the target input.
- Annealing: on retries, drop the distractor and replace with a compressed exemplar to coax brevity.

Task used for prototyping: meeting-notes -> action-items + priority + owner heuristics.
Why this task: semi-structured target reduces open-endedness and reveals hallucination and omission failures quickly.

Example staged few-shot sets (raw):
Stage 0 (Anchor & Distractors)
---
#BAD example (common failure: implicit owner hallucination)
Input: "Met with infra—Dave will look into the query perf and someone from security might follow up on IAM audit."
Output: "- Owner: Dave; Task: investigate query performance; Priority: High; Due: TBD"
Note: BAD because model confidently assigns 'security' follow-up to a named owner when not present.

#GOOD example (explicitly avoid hallucination)
Input: "Discussed query perf. Dave to investigate. Security team to review IAM audit (no owner named)."
Output: "- Owner: Dave | Task: Investigate query performance | Priority: High | Due: TBD
- Owner: (unassigned) | Task: Review IAM audit (security team) | Priority: Medium | Due: TBD"
Rationale: show unassigned owners for team-level items.

Stage 1 (Canonical Positive Set)
---
Input: "Sprint retro: UI lag reported by product; frontend to profile; backend might need batching. Action: create perf ticket and add repro steps."
Output: "- Owner: frontend-team | Task: Profile UI lag & gather repro steps | Priority: High | Due: next-sprint
- Owner: backend-team | Task: Consider batching to reduce latency | Priority: Medium | Due: TBD"

Stage 2 (Compression / Token-budget)
---
Input: "Customer call: fix crash in payments flow. Investigate logs, patch, verify."
Output: "- Owner: payments | Task: Fix crash; verify in staging | Priority: High"

Failure cases observed in ad-hoc runs:
- Hallucinated owners: model invents names when only teams referenced.
- Omitted items: when input is list-heavy, the model sometimes merges two adjacent bullets into one action incorrectly.
- Priority drift: model defaults to Medium for many things; needs heuristics for elevating severity based on keywords ("crash", "customer", "security").
- Token blowup: model includes entire quoted blocks from meeting notes verbatim rather than distilling.

Mitigations and prompt patterns to try: 
- Explicit "If owner not mentioned, set owner to (unassigned) and preserve team text" rule as an instruction line in the prompt.
- Use negative exemplars that show the wrong behavior and a single-line explanation after each negative exemplar: "Why wrong: assigns owner not present" (this helps demote the pattern).
- Post-process rule: if owner is a human name but not on allowed list, convert to "(unassigned)" and flag for manual review.
- Add keyword-weighted priority override: if input contains tokens in critical-set=[crash, data-loss, customer-impacts, production], set Priority=High.

Micro-benchmark plan (lightweight):
- Dataset: 120 meeting-note snippets sampled from internal retro notes + anonymized customer support summaries.
- Metrics: recall of discrete action items (precision/recall), hallucination rate (owner assigned when none present), average tokens per output, % of outputs flagged for manual review by heuristics.
- Baselines: static single-set few-shot (current), zero-shot instruction-only (fresh), staged-exemplar (this doc's method).
- Run config: 3 seeds, 10 samples per seed batching, measure variance.

Quick test templates (ad-hoc):
- Test 1: ambiguous-owner-case -> expect Owner: (unassigned) or team-level owner
- Test 2: adjacent-bullets-merge -> expect 2 separate action items, not merged
- Test 3: critical-keyword-elevation -> note with "customer blocked" should produce Priority: High

Prompts to prototype (skeletons)
- Full staged prompt skeleton:
""
"Task: Extract action items from meeting notes. Output each item on its own line using the format: - Owner: <owner> | Task: <short description> | Priority: <Low/Medium/High> | Due: <due or TBD>.
Instruction: If owner isn't explicitly named, set Owner to (unassigned); if the item refers to a team, preserve the team name.
Anchor: [BAD example + why wrong]
Positive examples: [3 canonical] 
Compression exemplar: [1 compressed example] 
Now extract items from the following input:
<INSERT INPUT>
""

- Minimal prompt alternative (for deployment): compress Stage 0/1 into 3 exemplars total; append a single-line rule for owner handling.

Rolling experiments / TODOs:
- [ ] Implement dataset of 120 anonymized snippets and label ground truth for items/owners/priorities. (Maya)
- [ ] Run micro-benchmark vs baseline and collect hallucination numbers. (Jordan)
- [ ] Try alternative negative-exemplar styles: 1) explicit label + explanation vs 2) counterfactual rewrite that fixes the mistake. (Priya)
- [ ] Evaluate token budget tradeoffs: run Stage 1 vs Stage1+Stage2 for 1k samples and measure delta in tokens per response. (Maya/Jordan)
- [ ] Add heuristic post-processing step to map informal owner mentions to canonical owner/team names using small alias dictionary.

Notes to self / rough observations:
- Negative exemplars feel powerful but increase prompt length; tradeoff with token cost needs to be measured.
- If model sees both bad+good, it sometimes flips to over-correction (becomes too conservative). Might need weight via ordering (bad before good) or explicit phrase: "Prefer patterns in GOOD examples."
- Consider a hybrid strategy: include 1 very short negative exemplar and 2 positives, then on retry replace negative with compressed positive to improve brevity.

Reference snippets (for quick copy-paste into runs):
- Ambiguous: "Talked about infra and ops. Alice to check logs; ops to follow up on rollbacks."
- Merge-risk: "Alice to draft runbook. Bob to review. Confirm ownership and staging plan."
- Critical keyword: "Payment gateway outage blocked customers; urgent rollback deployed; need RCA."

Session end notes: keep this lightweight; main deliverable = reproducible micro-benchmark and a small exemplar library (YAML/JSON) we can iterate on. Aim to have first-run numbers in 1 week.

-- Maya
